title: Race relations and Obama's campaign for the presidency, c2000–09

review.note: Original content following IAL Unit 3 Option 1D key topic 5.

learn.intro: By 2000 black Americans held thousands of elected offices and a black middle class had grown — yet tensions over policing, poverty and Hurricane Katrina showed how much remained unequal. How did Barack Obama win the presidency in 2008, and what did his victory mean?

sections.title: 1. Black voters and politicians at the turn of the century

blocks.p: The 2000 census counted about 36 million black Americans, around 12–13 per cent of the population. More than half lived in the South — reversing some of the earlier Great Migration as people moved to growing southern cities — with large concentrations in northern and western cities. Their votes were especially important in the South and in urban areas of swing states.

The number of black elected officials rose from fewer than 1,500 in 1970 to more than 9,000 by the early 2000s, helped by the Voting Rights Act and majority-black districts. Black mayors had led cities such as Atlanta, Detroit and Chicago; Colin Powell (2001–05) and Condoleezza Rice (2005–09) served as Secretary of State; Deval Patrick became Governor of Massachusetts in 2007.

A substantial black middle class had grown since the 1960s through education and professional and public-sector jobs, many moving to suburbs. But gaps in wealth, income, unemployment and poverty remained wide.

Continuing tensions included policing and racial profiling — riots followed a police shooting in Cincinnati in 2001; very high rates of imprisonment of black men; the slow federal response to Hurricane Katrina (2005), which hit black neighbourhoods of New Orleans hardest; and the Jena Six case (2006–07) in Louisiana.

sections.title: 2. Obama's political career to 2006

blocks.p: Barack Obama was born in Hawaii in 1961 to a Kenyan father and a white mother from Kansas. He worked as a community organiser in Chicago, studied at Harvard Law School, where in 1990 he became the first black president of the Harvard Law Review, and wrote the memoir Dreams from My Father (1995).

He served in the Illinois State Senate (1997–2004), lost a congressional primary to Bobby Rush in 2000, and in 2002 spoke against the coming war in Iraq. His keynote speech at the Democratic National Convention in July 2004 — insisting there was not a black America and a white America but a United States of America — made him a national figure. In November 2004 he was elected US Senator for Illinois with about 70 per cent of the vote, one of very few black senators in US history.

evidence: 1990: first black president of the Harvard Law Review.
November 2004: elected US Senator for Illinois.

blocks.p: Obama announced his candidacy in Springfield, Illinois, in February 2007. The favourite was Hillary Clinton. Obama won the Iowa caucuses in January 2008, proving he could win in an overwhelmingly white state, then built a delegate lead through caucus states and strong support from black voters in the South.

Reasons for success: his personality and rhetorical ability ('Yes we can'; 'change'); his early opposition to the Iraq war, which contrasted with Clinton's vote for it; a new election strategy using the internet and social networking to recruit volunteers and raise money from millions of small donors; a strong ground organisation in every state; and an appeal to young voters.

When sermons by his former pastor Jeremiah Wright caused controversy, Obama's 'A More Perfect Union' speech in Philadelphia (March 2008) addressed race directly and limited the damage. He secured the nomination in June 2008.

sections.title: 4. Victory in November 2008 and the response

blocks.p: Against the Republican John McCain, Obama benefited from the unpopularity of President George W. Bush and the Iraq war, and above all from the financial crisis: the collapse of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 shifted the campaign to the economy, where voters trusted Obama more. McCain's choice of Sarah Palin as running mate and his erratic response to the crisis hurt him. Obama raised far more money, having declined public funding for the general election.

On 4 November 2008 Obama won about 53 per cent of the popular vote and 365 electoral votes, carrying states such as Virginia, North Carolina and Indiana. Around 95 per cent of black voters, two-thirds of Latino and young voters, and about 43 per cent of white voters supported him; black turnout was very high.

The response: many black Americans saw the victory as the fulfilment of the movement's struggle; veterans such as John Lewis and Jesse Jackson spoke of it in those terms, and the night in Chicago's Grant Park became an iconic image. Many white Americans celebrated too. But there was also hostility: threats against the President-elect, the 'birther' conspiracy theory questioning his citizenship, and the rise of the Tea Party in 2009. Talk of a 'post-racial' America proved premature.

evidence: 4 November 2008: about 53% of the popular vote, 365 electoral votes.
About 95% of black voters and about 43% of white voters backed Obama.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence for why Obama won in November 2008.
evidence.model: The financial crisis after Lehman's collapse (September 2008); record fundraising; about 95% of black, 43% of white and two-thirds of young voters; 365 electoral votes.

evidence.q: Give precise evidence of continuing racial tension around 2000–09.
evidence.model: Cincinnati riots after a police shooting (2001); Hurricane Katrina (2005); the Jena Six case (2006–07); racial profiling and high imprisonment rates.

flashcards.q: Why did black voters matter politically around 2000?
flashcards.a: About 12–13% of the population, concentrated in the South and big cities — decisive in Democratic primaries and some swing states.

flashcards.q: Give evidence of the growth of black political office.
flashcards.a: Over 9,000 black elected officials by the early 2000s (under 1,500 in 1970); Powell and Rice as Secretary of State; Deval Patrick governor 2007.
National fame; a message of unity across race that later underpinned his crossover appeal.
flashcards.hint: Not a black America and a white America.

flashcards.q: Give four reasons Obama beat Clinton for the nomination.
flashcards.a: Rhetoric and personality; early opposition to the Iraq war; internet fundraising and organisation; caucus-state strategy; young and black voters.

flashcards.q: Why was the 'A More Perfect Union' speech important?
flashcards.a: It addressed race and the Wright controversy directly, limiting damage to his campaign.

flashcards.q: How did the financial crisis help Obama?
flashcards.a: It shifted the election to the economy, blamed on the Republican administration; McCain's response looked erratic.

flashcards.q: Give two responses to Obama's victory.
flashcards.a: Celebration as fulfilment of the civil rights struggle; hostility — threats, 'birther' conspiracy, the Tea Party.
